title: Time Saved Is Not a Measure - team review (18 changes)
summary:
Team you confirmed Tuesday morning ("Confirm as is"): Gloria Fenwick (adversarial, owns a 40-person landscaping supply business), Renee Calloway (who carries this?), Dr. Priya Raman (analytics, before-and-after studies), Tom Becker (sales operations). They reviewed YOUR interview draft (Time Saved Is Not a Measure) - not the old Prove the Delta idea. Each change is its own question; no recommendations. Nothing changes until you answer - the next run writes draft 2 with only what you accept.

Gloria's objection to the premise, in her words: "In my business, time saved is a measure. If my two counter people stop working Saturdays because AI writes the order confirmations, I stop paying overtime. That's a number on my P&L, not smoke."

Tom on what he'd keep: "Keep the boat anchor. That's the line people will repeat in meetings."

Items 4 and 14 both touch the 60-hour line from different sides. All four voices in full: the link below.

questions.text: 1. Say that in a small business, time saved can be a real measure (overtime cut, Saturdays off) - "catching smoke" fits companies with finance teams, not every reader (Gloria Fenwick)

2. Don't open the four-teams answer with "they should be taking 20 more calls" - output depends on demand the employee doesn't control; lead with the upstream / whole value stream look (Gloria Fenwick)

3. Restate Greg's example in output terms (patterns shipped per week, meetings booked) - as written, "5 a week vs 1, 20 weeks vs 4" measures time, the thing the pattern says not to measure (Gloria Fenwick)
4. Drop or make generic the Anthropic employee's 60-hour post and "that is not possible" - it reads like a fight with a stranger and dates the page (Gloria Fenwick)
5. Name the one measure a reader picks first on Monday, so "teach them to fish" comes with a first step (Gloria Fenwick)
6. Say you need a "before" number (baseline), and if you don't have one, start counting now (Renee Calloway)
7. Say who finds the "10 hours of organizational value" - the manager - instead of "it is on us" (Renee Calloway)
8. Add the "Who owns the work / What you stop doing" lines: who owns the output measure and the backlog; what stops - the "how many hours did AI save you?" survey (Renee Calloway)
9. Add one line on keeping a ready list of valuable work, so the manager isn't inventing the 10 hours on the spot (Renee Calloway)
10. Compare output to the same period last year or to a team not using AI yet, so the season or a price change doesn't get credited to AI (Dr. Priya Raman)
11. Present "10 hours saved = 20 more calls" as the question to ask ("where did the 10 hours go?"), not the expected answer - saved time rarely converts one-for-one (Dr. Priya Raman)
12. Pair every output measure with a guard measure - calls per week plus customer satisfaction; quotes per week plus win rate (Dr. Priya Raman)
13. In the example, say how you know the meeting wouldn't have happened yet (the dates on the results page), so readers ask the same of their own claims (Dr. Priya Raman)
14. Make the point of the 60-hour claim that it measures input - not whether it's possible (Dr. Priya Raman)
15. Add a line on tying a revenue or time-to-market claim to something that wouldn't have happened otherwise - point to Greg's meeting example as the test (Tom Becker)
16. Say a meeting in the pipeline isn't worth the whole deal - finance discounts it by how often meetings become deals; don't put a deal value on a first meeting (Tom Becker)
17. Add how to ask about time saved so people keep reporting it - reward the output, don't punish the honesty (Tom Becker)
18. Keep the boat-anchor line and move it near the top (Tom Becker)

Lead [Synthesized]: "Time saved is never time earned when left unclaimed. Measure what the saved time produced - more output, faster to market, happier customers - and make sure there's valuable work waiting to fill it."
When to use it [Synthesized]: "any time someone reports AI time savings, or asks for budget based on them."
Level (the site's three levels are Foundation, Practice, Leadership)
Category - Accuracy was kept from Prove the Delta
